source_prose_budget: Annotations are deliberately concise. Reuse rather than duplicate source-derived prose; default web allowance is 200 words per source across final artifacts.

sources.title: Understanding beginners’ mistakes with Haskell
sources.population: Mostly second–fourth-year university students with prior introductory programming.
sources.design: Eight-week elective; automatic error classification plus instructor/assistant manual session coding.
sources.findings: CouldntMatch occurred for 53/55 students. Of sessions with that error, 69% involved type confusion and roughly 30% precedence; one-third of type-confusion sessions came from one deliberately type-focused task. Missing recursive cases occurred, but authors did not observe the specific base-case-as-stopping-condition misconception. They reported no conceptual partial-application difficulty and little early laziness difficulty; syntax remained problematic.
sources.limitations: Single cohort; coding infers intent from submissions; outside help and exploratory incomplete code possible; task exposure changes over time; no causal instructional comparison.
provenance: Targeted web search: Haskell negative transfer students study
Backward references: Chambers2012, Clack1995, Segal1994, Heeren2003

sources.title: Investigating Compilation Errors of Students Learning Haskell
sources.population: First-year ELTE undergraduates; basic imperative experience in a statically typed language.
sources.design: Submission logs, nine teaching weeks; sampled manual root-cause classification and response/correction times.
sources.findings: Among sampled type-related errors: list/scalar/dimensional mismatch 20%; missing argument 8.6%; simple type mismatch 8.6%; wrong operation 8.4%; grouping/precedence 6.7%. Type errors predominated after initial weeks and were slower to repair. Some syntax mistakes produced misleading name/type diagnostics.
sources.limitations: Error proportions are not learner prevalence. Anonymous sessions cannot track individuals across semester; instructor coding may misclassify intent; one curriculum. Only eventually fixed errors enter correction-time analysis.
provenance: Web query: Haskell students misconceptions empirical learning functional programming difficulties
Backward references: Singer2018, Heeren2003, AskElle2017

sources.title: Functional Baby Talk: Analysis of Code Fragments from Novice Haskell Programmers
sources.population: 2016 Glasgow/FutureLearn MOOC users; prior background heterogeneous, not individually verified.
sources.design: Logs; expressions reparsed; sessions inferred by IP and ten-minute gaps.
sources.findings: Observed parenthesis, let/where, do-block binding/final-expression and range-notation errors. Unsupported data/type/multiline definitions were also attempted. About 100K inputs copied tutorial code versus 60K original, demonstrating why activity counts alone are weak learning measures.
sources.limitations: One course, IP proxy and browser/OS selection; tool rejects some valid Haskell. Parsing failures do not establish a stable conceptual misconception or prevalence among unique learners.
provenance: Initial targeted web search
Backward snowball from Nemeth2019 reference3

sources.title: Helium, for Learning Haskell
sources.population: University introductory functional-programming courses; exact student count not extracted.
sources.design: Compiler/tool experience report and seven-week compilation logs.
sources.findings: 31.6% of compilation attempts produced type errors; 46.3% were accepted. Undefined names dominated other static errors. Tool supplies source-oriented diagnostics and heuristics for swapped/missing arguments and related-function confusion.
sources.limitations: Compiler acceptance is not task correctness or learning. Course/tasks and subset affect frequencies. Positive instructor/student feedback has no controlled learning comparison; undefined names include typos, so they do not establish scope misconceptions.
provenance: Backward reference from Nemeth2019 reference4
Targeted web query: Haskell types students Helium study

sources.title: How Type Errors Were Fixed and What Students Did?
sources.population: Three university Haskell cohorts (2002,2003,2017), including first-year learners.
sources.design: Retrospective program-sequence and repair analysis; manually identified intended fixes.
sources.findings: Over 45% of final type-error fixes in each dataset added/removed parentheses or brackets. Wrong annotations appeared in 28%,34.4%,27% of analyzed errors. Actual fixes often differ from the location suggested by diagnostics. Type signatures may be initially wrong or become stale after definition changes.
sources.limitations: Not every original ill-typed program analyzed: 1000 sampled of 2000 in first dataset. Approximately 6% lacked usable reference repair and were excluded. Repair sequences support behavior, not direct mental-model diagnoses. Cohort/task/compiler differences.
provenance: Targeted web query: How Type Errors Were Fixed pdf
Sider DOI lookup confirmed bibliographic record
Backward references shared Helium/Tirronen corpora

sources.title: Structural versus Pipeline Composition of Higher-Order Functions (Experience Report)
sources.population: Accelerated introductory CS students after higher-order-function reading/assignment.
sources.language: Racket Advanced Student Language; pure setting
sources.design: Seven input-output planning problems; same operator pairs structural/pipeline; partly randomized order; five-day response window.
sources.findings: Apparently correct narrative structural compositions:37,31,31; pipeline:22,10 for first two problems. Third pipeline problem admitted an unintended simpler solution. Some students treated map as fold, confused filter/take-while, or could not infer intermediate transformations.
sources.limitations: Small single-institution task study; no Haskell/static-checker test. Input-output ambiguity, first structural question fixed, nonmandatory surveillance, and unintended solutions limit generalization. Difficulty comparison is task-specific; pedagogic sequencing remains a hypothesis.
provenance: Root SciSpace lead
Primary author manuscript found by exact-title web search
Reference list traces Krishnamurthi/Fisler2021 and Rivera/Goldstone planning work
sources.transfer_boundary: Pure list/HOF composition transfers conceptually; Haskell currying/laziness/types were not measured.

sources.title: Plan Composition Using Higher-Order Functions
sources.population: Selective US university placement/accelerated CS module; ~90% prior computing, nearly all new to FP.
sources.design: HOF recognition, behavioral explanations, planning then programming; month-long placement module.
sources.findings: Only 10/402 plans were explicitly wrong; most implementations passed instructor tests. Composition-recognition errors often omitted an outer map, treating nested inputs as flattened examples. Understanding single HOFs did not imply identical performance across representations.
sources.limitations: No control group or retention/transfer test; high selectivity/prior experience; ceiling effects; author coding and tool affordances affect interpretation. Plan success does not prove planning intervention caused learning.
provenance: Companion/citation-chain search from Rivera2022 structural
Exact-title primary author page and PDF
sources.transfer_boundary: HOF planning in Racket; efficacy for Haskell learners untested.

sources.title: Goanna: a novel approach for automated type error debugging
sources.population: Historical Helium student-program corpus; current learner study planned.
sources.design: Corpus diagnostic accuracy and generated performance benchmarks; no completed rigorous learner experiment.
sources.findings: Reports diagnostic accuracy 81.6% Goanna versus 65.5% Helium and 33.7% GHC. Preliminary workshop reactions were positive; rigorous human evaluation is future work.
sources.limitations: Accuracy is a tool-performance outcome, not evidence of conceptual learning, retention, transfer or debugging independence. Historical corpus, supported-language subset, and computational cost constrain applicability.

Publisher primary full text

sources.title: GeckoGraph: A visual language for polymorphic types
sources.population: Haskell Reddit/Discord volunteers; self-rated expertise, not a classroom sample.
sources.design: Preregistered ten-task gamified experiment; counterbalanced groups alternate graphical/text notation at odd/even levels.
sources.findings: No overall significant time/success advantage. Beginner aggregate success95.12% versus92.68%,p=.0431. Task10 beginner success94.9% versus80.4%,p=.0452:14.5 percentage points. Familiar task10 difference11.2points has p=.136.
sources.limitations: Reported N contradicts subgroup totals; Shapiro-Wilk interpretation is reversed; familiar task10 rejection claim contradicts p=.136. Repeated-task dependence/multiple comparisons require scrutiny. Artificial tasks, skips, self-selection, ceiling effects; performance with aid is not retained learning.
